essays.q: How does a microcontroller differ from a microprocessor?
essays.sol: A microcontroller includes many elements of a computer system, whereas a microprocessor is only the CPU.

essays.q: What are some common functional units found in a typical microcontroller?
essays.sol: The processor core, ROM, RAM, one or more hardware peripherals, a signal-connection block between the functional blocks and an external memory controller.

essays.q: Discuss an advantage and disadvantage of multifunctional pins on a microcontroller.
essays.sol: Advantage: it reduces the number of pins and the physical size of the device. Disadvantage: it is not always possible to use every microcontroller feature an application needs, so the design may require additional external hardware.

essays.q: Which peripherals allow a microcontroller to interact with the real world?
essays.sol: Timers, ADCs, DACs, communication controllers, GPIOs, quadrature encoders and PWMs.

essays.q: How does an embedded system differ from a personal computer system?
essays.sol: An embedded system is designed to interact directly with the real world and perform a specific function; a personal computer processes data and can be configured with application software to perform a number of tasks.

essays.q: Identify some types of embedded systems in which microcontrollers are found.
essays.sol: Personal electronics, consumer electronics, automotive systems and communication devices (and automation and robotics).

essays.q: What is a SoC?
essays.sol: A SoC is a system chip, a complete computer on a single silicon chip.

essays.q: What are two important advantages of a SoC?
essays.sol: Small size and reduced power consumption.

essays.q: List the functional elements of a SoC.
essays.sol: One or more processor cores; a DSP; a GPU; memory; ADC and DAC; I/O interfaces; timing sources; power management; bus bridges; peripherals; and programmable logic.

essays.q: State seven things to do when handling and transporting static-sensitive devices, and explain why a person walking over a wool/nylon carpet can damage a VLSI microprocessor. Use the numbers of Tables 12.1 and 12.2.
essays.sol: Seven things: a grounded wrist strap with a 1 MΩ resistor; heel straps; static-dissipative floor and bench mats; avoiding very dry environments; ground jacks; grounded test equipment; low-voltage grounded soldering irons (also anti-static IC tools, avoiding high-voltage sources, anti-static packaging). Walking over a wool/nylon carpet at 20 % humidity generates up to 35 kV (Table 12.1) while a VLSI microprocessor withstands only 20 V to 100 V (Table 12.2): at least 350 times the top of its range; at 80 % humidity it is still 1.5 kV, still 15 times.

essays.q: Determine the values of the external resistors for a 555 timer used as an astable multivibrator with an output frequency of 10 kHz, if the external capacitor C is 0.004 µF and the duty cycle is to be approximately 80%.
essays.sol: Floyd 7-6: $f=\dfrac{1.44}{(R_1+2R_2)C}$ and $D=\dfrac{R_1+R_2}{R_1+2R_2}$. $R_1+2R_2=1.44/(10\text{ kHz}\times 0.004\,\mu\text{F})$ = 36 kΩ; $R_1+R_2=0.8\times 36$ = 28.8 kΩ, so $R_2$ = 7.2 kΩ and $R_1$ = 21.6 kΩ. With standard E24 values $R_1$ = 22 kΩ, $R_2$ = 7.5 kΩ: $f$ = 9.73 kHz, $D$ = 79.7 %. The printed answer R1 = 9.1 kΩ, R2 = 4.3 kΩ gives $f$ = 20.3 kHz and $D$ = 75.7 % with C = 0.004 µF; they give 10 kHz only if C ≈ 0.008 µF. The printed statement and the printed answer contradict each other; the site uses the values computed from the statement.

essays.q: How many flip-flops are required to implement each of the following in a Johnson counter configuration: (a) modulus-4 (b) modulus-8 (c) modulus-12 (d) modulus-18?
essays.sol: A Johnson counter of n flip-flops steps through 2n states, so modulus = 2n and the number of flip-flops = modulus / 2: (a) 4/2 = 2, (b) 8/2 = 4, (c) 12/2 = 6, (d) 18/2 = 9. This agrees with the printed answer.

essays.q: In the counter of Problem 4, assume that each flip-flop has a propagation delay from the triggering edge of the clock to a change in the Q output of 8 ns. Determine the worst-case (longest) delay time from a clock pulse to the arrival of the counter in a given state. Specify the state or states for which this worst-case delay occurs.
essays.sol: In a ripple counter each stage changes only after the previous one has changed, so the settling time of a transition is 8 ns times the position of the highest stage that toggles. The worst case is when all three stages change: 011 → 100 and 111 → 000, i.e. 3 × 8 ns = 24 ns (arriving at states 100 and 000). This agrees with the printed answer.

essays.q: If the counter of Problem 5 were synchronous rather than asynchronous, what would be the longest delay time?
essays.sol: In a synchronous counter all flip-flops receive the clock together, so the outputs change after a single propagation delay: the longest time is only 8 ns (instead of 24 ns). This agrees with the printed answer.

essays.q: A 4-bit ripple counter uses J-K flip-flops with a 15 ns propagation delay and a 1 MHz clock. (a) Modulus? (b) Total settling time when it recycles? (c) Maximum clock frequency? (d) Frequency of the last-stage output?
essays.sol: (a) $2^4$ = 16. (b) 4 × 15 ns = 60 ns. (c) $f_{max}=1/60\text{ ns}$ = 16.67 MHz. (d) 1 MHz / 16 = 62.5 kHz. The 1 μs clock period exceeds 60 ns so the counter works correctly.

essays.s: Added · BCD counter from a binary counter
essays.q: Design a BCD (modulus-10) counter from a 4-bit binary counter with asynchronous reset: (a) how many flip-flops? (b) which state triggers the reset? (c) how long does state 1010 exist? (d) with a 100 kHz clock, what is the output frequency of the last stage of the modulus-10 counter?
essays.sol: (a) $2^3=8<10\le 2^4$ so 4 flip-flops. (b) Decode 1010 (ten) with a two-input NAND on Q1 and Q3 (the 1s of 1010) and connect it to the CLR inputs of all flip-flops. (c) Only a glitch, about a NAND-gate delay plus the clear time of the flip-flop (tens of ns): a hazard to be aware of. (d) The output period of the 10-state sequence is 10 clock pulses: 100 kHz / 10 = 10 kHz (Q3 is not symmetric: HIGH for 2 pulses, LOW for 8).

essays.q: A 555 astable has R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 2 kΩ, C = 0.1 μF. Find $t_H$, $t_L$, the period, the frequency and the duty cycle. What must change to get a duty cycle below 50 %?
essays.sol: $t_H=0.7(R_1+R_2)C$ = 210 μs; $t_L=0.7R_2C$ = 140 μs; $T$ = 350 μs; $f$ = 2.857 kHz; duty = 60 %. For a duty cycle below 50 % add a diode across R2 (Floyd Figure 7-59) so that C charges through R1 only and discharges through R2, with R1 smaller than R2.

essays.q: An 8-bit shift-right register holds 00000000. The sequence 11010010 is entered serially (right-most bit first) at the left end with a 250 kHz clock. (a) The contents after each pulse (list them). (b) The entry time. (c) If this register is used as a delay line for a serial signal, what is the delay?
essays.sol: (a) 00000000; 10000000; 01000000; 00100000; 10010000; 01001000; 10100100; 11010010. (b) 8 × 4 μs = 32 μs. (c) Each bit passes through 8 stages so the delay equals the entry time = 32 μs.

essays.q: Tabulate the first 8 pulses of a 4-flip-flop Johnson counter starting at 0000 and of a 4-flip-flop ring counter starting at 1000. Compare their moduli and the number of gates needed to decode each state.
essays.sol: Johnson: 0000 → 1000 → 1100 → 1110 → 1111 → 0111 → 0011 → 0001 → 0000. Ring: 1000 → 0100 → 0010 → 0001 → 1000 → 0100 → 0010 → 0001 → 1000. Johnson modulus = 8 (2n), ring = 4 (n). Each Johnson state decodes with one two-input AND gate (only two adjacent stages matter); a ring state is read directly from one output, no gate.

essays.s: Added · XOR in a PAL and a LUT
essays.q: A function $F=\overline{A}B+A\overline{B}$ (XOR) is to be built in a PAL. (a) How many product terms? (b) Which links must the fuse map keep? (c) What does a 2-input LUT hold to implement the same function?
essays.sol: (a) Two product terms, $\overline{A}B$ and $A\overline{B}$, feeding a fixed OR gate. (b) Term 1 keeps the links from $\overline{A}$ and $B$ (the other fuses are blown); term 2 keeps those from $A$ and $\overline{B}$. (c) A 4-cell LUT for AB = 00, 01, 10, 11 holds 0, 1, 1, 0.

essays.q: Your aircraft flies at 240 kt and an intruder flies head-on along the same track at 240 kt, now 8 NM away. (a) The closure rate? (b) The time to the closest point of approach? (c) Which data does TCAS not need to compute this alert? (d) If TCAS issues an RA, what must the pilot do?
essays.sol: (a) 240 + 240 = 480 kt. (b) $\tau=8/480$ h = 60 s. (c) Neither bearing nor heading is needed, only distance and closure rate (Tooley 15.8). (d) Disengage the autopilot, fly the pitch command manually, and ignore flight-director and ATC advisories if necessary; the RA has the highest priority.

essays.q: An accelerometer along the track reads 1.5 m/s² for 40 s from rest. (a) The velocity? (b) The distance? (c) If the acceleration data has a constant error of 0.01 m/s², what are the velocity and distance errors after 40 s? (d) Why does this explain the need for accurate initialisation and GPS aiding?
essays.sol: (a) $v=at=60$ m/s. (b) $s=\tfrac12at^2=1200$ m. (c) Velocity error $0.01\times40=0.4$ m/s; distance error $\tfrac12\times0.01\times40^2=8$ m, growing with $t^2$. (d) Errors accumulate with time, so the initial datum must be accurate (Tooley 15.7); GPS supplies additional information (not operationally necessary).

essays.q: GPS: (a) Convert the orbit height of 20,200 km to nautical miles. (b) Compute the period of a circular orbit at that height (Earth radius 6,371 km, $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}$ m³/s²) and compare it with Tooley's 12 hours. (c) How many chips does the 1.023 MHz C/A code, repeating every 1 ms, contain? (d) Name the three GPS segments.
essays.sol: (a) 20,200 / 1.852 = 10,907 NM (Tooley rounds to 10,900). (b) $r=26571$ km; $T=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/\mu}$ = 43,105 s = 11.97 hours ≈ 12 hours: it agrees. (c) $1.023\times10^6\times10^{-3}$ = 1,023 chips. (d) Space, user and control.

essays.q: An AFDX VL has a maximum frame length of 1,518 bytes. (a) The maximum bit rate with a BAG of 4 ms. (b) An avionics port supplies data 150 times a second: what is the largest BAG you can choose? (c) What is then the maximum bit rate of the VL? (d) The time to transmit one longest frame on a 100 Mbit/s network?
essays.sol: (a) $1518\times8\times1000/4$ = 3,036,000 bit/s ≈ 3 Mbit/s (Tooley 16.8). (b) It must be at least 150 Hz: 125 Hz (8 ms) is not enough, 250 Hz (4 ms) is, so BAG = 4 ms. (c) 3,036,000 bit/s. (d) $1518\times8/10^8$ = 121.44 μs.

essays.q: Check the arithmetic of the Tooley AFDX frame: (a) Compute the minimum and maximum frame length (excluding the preamble, SFD and inter-frame gap) from the fields: MAC destination 6, MAC source 6, Type 2, IP 20, UDP 8, payload 1 to 1,471, padding, SN 1, FCS 4. (b) When is padding needed and how many bytes at most? (c) The transmit time of the maximum frame on a 10 Mbit/s network?
essays.sol: (a) Minimum 6 + 6 + 2 + 20 + 8 + 17 + 1 + 4 = 64 bytes (payload plus padding of at least 17); maximum 6 + 6 + 2 + 20 + 8 + 1,471 + 1 + 4 = 1518 bytes. (b) When the payload is below 17 bytes; at most 16 bytes of padding (a 1-byte payload needs 16). (c) $1518\times8/(10\times10^6)$ = 1.2144 ms; adding the 8-byte preamble and the 12-byte gap gives $(1518+20)\times8/10^7$ = 1.2304 ms.

essays.q: Compare the federated and IMA architectures on the four criteria of Tooley (Table 18.1): processing, data interconnection and cabling, application software, suppliers. State five benefits of IMA.
essays.sol: Federated: many embedded computers dedicated to separate functions; many low and medium speed buses (ARINC 429, 629); software resident on each LRU, physically firewalled; restricted suppliers. IMA: centralised processing on a shared, partitioned platform; a common high-speed switched backbone (ARINC 664/AFDX); logically firewalled software; ideally open source, multiple sources. Benefits: manage many functions at once, lighter cabling (fuel, environment, cost), support for new functions (aircraft condition monitoring), multi-source support (flexibility, faster development), fewer spares and less single-source dependence.

essays.q: Let p = 1100 and q = 0101 (4-bit vectors). Using the VHDL precedence (NOT > shift/rotate > AND/OR/XOR): (a) p AND q; (b) NOT p AND q; (c) NOT (p AND q); (d) p XOR q; (e) explain why (b) and (c) differ.
essays.sol: (a) 0100. (b) NOT p = 0011, AND q = 0001. (c) p AND q = 0100, NOT = 1011. (d) 1001. (e) In (b) NOT applies only to p because it has the highest precedence; in (c) the brackets change the order so NOT applies to the result of the AND.

essays.q: Write (in correct VHDL syntax) the entity declaration and behavioural architecture for a half adder with an active-LOW enable EN. Give the truth table and state the change from Tooley's active-HIGH version.
essays.sol: ENTITY half_adder IS PORT (x, y, en : IN bit; sum, carry : OUT bit); END half_adder; ARCHITECTURE behaviour OF half_adder IS BEGIN PROCESS (x, y, en) BEGIN IF en = '0' THEN sum <= x XOR y; carry <= x AND y; ELSE sum <= '0'; carry <= '0'; END IF; END PROCESS; END behaviour; Truth table: EN = 0 gives (sum, carry) = (x XOR y, x AND y) for the four (x, y) combinations: 00 gives (0,0), 01 gives (1,0), 10 gives (1,0), 11 gives (0,1); EN = 1 gives (0,0) for every (x, y). The only change: the condition IF en = '1' becomes IF en = '0' (Test Your Understanding 17.3). Note: the book prints "PROCESS (x; y)", "ELSEIF" and "3 down to 0" (the correct forms are commas, ELSIF and "3 downto 0").

essays.q: A VHDL model of an XOR gate has gate_delay = 15 ns and input a changes at t = 100 ns (0 to 1) while b = 0. (a) When does output c change? (b) A half adder built from three gates 7408, 7404, 7408 (15 ns each) has what total delay at the Sum output? (c) Why simulate the delay before manufacture?
essays.sol: (a) c <= (a xor b) after gate_delay so c changes (0 to 1) at 100 + 15 = 115 ns. (b) 3 × 15 = 45 ns. (c) In high-speed circuits the spurious transient states caused by delay can produce unpredictable behaviour; simulation with a test bench lets you check and refine before manufacture (Tooley 17.9, 17.10).

essays.q: A 4.7 GB film (1 GB = 10⁹ bytes) must be loaded into the IFE memory. (a) The loading time over a 100 Mbit/s link and over 1 Gbit/s (ignoring overhead). (b) If an aircraft loads 8 such films one after another over Gigabit, the total time? (c) Why does Tooley say Gigabit Ethernet is preferred?
essays.sol: (a) $t=4.7\times8\times10^9/10^8$ = 376 s ≈ 6.3 min; at 1 Gbit/s: 37.6 s. (b) 8 × 37.6 s = 300.8 s ≈ 5.0 min. (c) Digital media files are large so the link must be very fast; 100 Mbit/s suffices but is ten times slower (Tooley 19.3).

essays.q: The low cabin chime is a 494 Hz sine wave, the high chime 587 Hz, each lasting 900 ms. (a) The period of each tone. (b) The number of cycles in one chime. (c) State the four chime signals of Tooley's convention and where they are sent from.
essays.sol: (a) $T_{low}=1/494$ = 2.024 ms; $T_{high}=1/587$ = 1.704 ms. (b) 494 × 0.9 = 444.6 cycles; 587 × 0.9 = 528.3 cycles. (c) Passenger call: a single high tone from seats and toilets to the cabin crew; attendant call: high/low between cabin crew stations; attendant emergency call: high/low repeated three times from the flight crew to the cabin crew; seat belt sign: a single low tone.

essays.q: Compare portable and installed EFB on four criteria: whether part of the type design, whether certification is needed, the hardware, an example. State the difference between Type A and Type B EFB applications with examples.
essays.sol: Portable: not part of the type design whether or not it leaves the aircraft; no certification; a tablet or laptop on battery or aircraft power; e.g. iPad, Surface Pro; supports Type A or B applications. Installed: part of the type design (or an official alteration); needs certification; two display units DU on the side consoles, each linked to an EU in the avionics bay (B777: two single-board computers, Linux and Windows). Type A: browsers and readers of standard documents (PDF, XML, HTML), failure has no safety effect. Type B: mass and balance, performance tools, moving maps, no airworthiness approval but the operator must carry out an assessment.
